title: Is "Daggermouth" the First Bestselling AI Novel?
excerpt: Daggermouth could be the first best-selling novel partly written by a chatbot.
content_html:
Most self-published authors can only dream of writing something as popular as Daggermouth. Set in a surveillance state ruled by a masked elite, the novel traces the unlikely romance between the president’s son and an assassin hired to kill him. Since H. M. Wolfe uploaded Daggermouth to Amazon as a Kindle ebook, it has been a viral hit. “Did I finish Daggermouth, or did Daggermouth finish me?” a TikTok book influencer gushed. In February, Simon & Schuster paid seven figures to secure the publishing rights to the book and its sequel, which is due out next year.

Daggermouth has spent months on USA Today’s best-seller list and is ranked No. 1 in Amazon’s “science-fiction romance” genre. It also tops a less prestigious list, one compiled by academics studying AI writing. Among thousands of self-published Amazon ebooks that they identified as containing “substantial AI text,” none was more popular than Daggermouth.

Until recently, AI fiction has been easy to dismiss as slop. On Amazon, new-book releases nearly tripled from 2022 to 2025. (That’s probably not because humans suddenly dedicated themselves en masse to the written word.) Many are blatant copycats of existing titles, seemingly intended to trick readers into buying them. Their sales figures are generally meager; the reviews, indignant. A suspicious number of them feature protagonists with the same names. Last year, readers of one fantasy novel noticed a line that seemed to be responding to a prompt asking a chatbot to write in the style of another author. But if a book as beloved as Daggermouth were written with a chatbot, it would raise an awkward question: Could AI fiction be getting … good?

In a new study, researchers randomly selected more than 14,000 Kindle ebooks and ran them through Pangram, an AI-detection tool. One in five came back as more than 25 percent AI-written; Daggermouth returned 60 percent, according to an underlying data set that the authors shared with me. Those numbers, they acknowledge, tell us only so much. The researchers grouped together text that Pangram had flagged as either “AI-generated” or “moderately AI-assisted” (the latter of which can mean that AI was used to edit or polish human writing, or vice versa). And although Pangram has a low rate of false positives, it is not perfect.

Read: America has a Pangram problem

So the study’s authors, led by Tuhin Chakrabarty, a professor of computer science at Stony Brook University, devised another check. They scanned each book’s text for “rare expressions”—strings of at least five words in a specific order—that also appear in other suspected AI books but almost never in human-written ones. Daggermouth had many of them. For instance, the following sentence appears near the end of a multipage sex scene in Chapter 27: “They collapsed together, a tangle of sweat-slicked limbs and racing hearts.” That same sentence, word for word, also shows up in another self-published ebook by a different author. Or consider this line from Chapter 38 of Daggermouth: “Her pulse thundered in her ears, drowning out the murmurs of the crowd.” It’s also in an ebook by another author who has published more than 400 different titles on Amazon in the past three years.

The study has yet to be peer-reviewed, and to be clear, there is no definitive proof that Wolfe used AI. “The suggestion that I used generative AI to write Daggermouth is wholly untrue,” Wolfe said in a statement sent by her lawyer. “I wrote this book myself. I have been outspoken about my opposition to generative AI and what it’s doing to writers, artists, and the creative community. I don’t believe it belongs in the writing process.” Referencing Pangram’s limitations, Wolfe added that “accusations like these have real consequences for authors, and they should not be made on the basis of technology that is known to be unreliable.” Susannah Lawrence, a spokesperson for Daggermouth’s publisher, Simon & Schuster, told me in an email that the company stands behind the book, noting that it went through “the same editorial and production process as our other published titles.” Neither Wolfe nor Lawrence addressed my questions about the “rare expressions” that Daggermouth shares with other recent ebooks.

Chakrabarty, who researches AI writing, told me that Daggermouth has “too many telltale signs” of AI for him to buy that explanation. He cited Chapter 18, “Thank You,” as an example: His research team broke it into 12 chunks for Pangram to evaluate, and the tool classified all parts as AI-generated. (In my own spot checks, the tool classified the first few paragraphs as human-written and the rest of the chapter as 100 percent AI.) I ran this by Mohit Iyyer, a professor of computer science at the University of Maryland who wasn’t involved with the study. An expert on AI-language detection, Iyyer told me that even accounting for Pangram’s fallibility, it’s “almost statistically impossible” for an entirely human-written book to register as 60 percent AI. He added that the study’s broader methodology, which connects AI writing to ebook sales, is sound.

Whether or not you believe that Wolfe deserves the benefit of the doubt, the same questions about how Daggermouth was written apply to a growing number of other hits on Amazon. Chakrabarty’s study found that books written with “substantial” AI assistance made up 20 percent of Amazon’s ebook catalog, 12 percent of sales, and 10 percent of best sellers in their genre.

Yet Daggermouth stands out for more than just its popularity. The second-best-selling ebook in the data set is Inked Athena, by Nicole Fox, an author who has 418 titles listed on Amazon. Daggermouth, in contrast, appears to be one of just two novels to Wolfe’s name in 2025, and its sequel is not due out until 2027—an indication that Wolfe’s process likely involves significant amounts of genuine human craft. Iyyer said that using AI in a way that results in a novel that’s actually enjoyable to read takes “a huge amount of effort by a human author.”

Read: The future of writing is a lot like hip-hop

Another difference: Jennifer Prokop, who reviews books for Kirkus and co-hosts Fated Mates, a popular podcast about romance novels, told me that people in her world keep talking about Daggermouth. “Nicole Fox, I’ve never heard a single soul talk about her,” she said. (Fox did not respond to a request for comment.) Prokop sees mechanical prose cropping up mostly in self-published ebooks, for which the dominant platform is Amazon’s Kindle Unlimited subscription service. Just because an ebook is charting on Kindle doesn’t mean people are devouring it. Grifters can now use AI to crank out titles by the dozen and then use all kinds of tricks to entice readers, such as buying hundreds of bogus five-star reviews and paying click farms to juice their metrics. “If you can get 10,000 people to read 10 pages of your book, and you have 300 books you’re putting out,” she said, you can make real money. “But you’re not actually writing romances people want to read.” (Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.)

If Daggermouth is AI, then maybe it’s just an outlier—a book that caught the perfect wave of social-media hype. (A series of controversies surrounding the book, including accusations of the author’s AI use and a backlash to the cover art for a special hardcover version, seemed to galvanize its fans and bring it even more attention.) The notion that AI writing requires a perfect confluence of events to top the charts is a comforting thought. But it might not be true. “Everyone thinks they can tell AI writing,” Christine Larson, a journalism professor at the University of Colorado at Boulder who studies the effect of technology on creative work, told me. “But I don’t think we can tell so much.” Privately, several authors and editors have told her that they’re using the technology to accelerate or improve their output. “I totally buy into the idea that a human working with AI can write something that is compelling,” she said. “I have absolutely no doubt that we will see more of this in the future.”

If she’s right, then the question is not about whether we’ll see AI best sellers. It’s about whether anyone involved with them will admit it. Coral Hart, a South African author who uses AI to help her publish hundreds of books a year under different pen names, told me that she works hard to keep her pseudonyms secret after she received death threats and thousands of one-star reviews following a New York Times story about her. Hart claimed that she has had successful authors join the classes that she teaches on AI writing, though she declined to name them. “Until they stop the bullying, the witch hunts, and the ousting, I don’t think authors are going to be transparent, and I don’t blame them,” Hart said. “I’m certainly not going to.”

The taboo against the use of AI in literature is understandable: Among other things, it’s wrong to take credit for a book that you didn’t write yourself. Shunning authors suspected of employing AI might work if there were any way to tell for sure—which there isn’t. That shaming ritual puts the moral burden on individual authors instead of on the mammoth corporations responsible for the system in which they’re trying to eke out a livelihood. It also tends to collapse any distinction between pure AI slop and human writing that is assisted by AI. The upshot is a state of affairs that feels untenable: AI writing can be lucrative, but only if it’s kept secret. Eventually, something’s got to give.

I don’t believe it belongs in the writing process.” Referencing Pangram’s limitations, Wolfe added that “accusations like these have real consequences for authors, and they should not be made on the basis of technology that is known to be unreliable.” Susannah Lawrence, a spokesperson for Daggermouth’s publisher, Simon & Schuster, told me in an email that the company stands behind the book, noting that it went through “the same editorial and production process as our other published titles.” Neither Wolfe nor Lawrence addressed my questions about the “rare expressions” that Daggermouth shares with other recent ebooks.

blocks.html_en: Chakrabarty, who researches AI writing, told me that Daggermouth has “too many telltale signs” of AI for him to buy that explanation. He cited Chapter 18, “Thank You,” as an example: His research team broke it into 12 chunks for Pangram to evaluate, and the tool classified all parts as AI-generated. (In my own spot checks, the tool classified the first few paragraphs as human-written and the rest of the chapter as 100 percent AI.) I ran this by Mohit Iyyer, a professor of computer science at the University of Maryland who wasn’t involved with the study. An expert on AI-language detection, Iyyer told me that even accounting for Pangram’s fallibility, it’s “almost statistically impossible” for an entirely human-written book to register as 60 percent AI. He added that the study’s broader methodology, which connects AI writing to ebook sales, is sound.

blocks.html_en: Whether or not you believe that Wolfe deserves the benefit of the doubt, the same questions about how Daggermouth was written apply to a growing number of other hits on Amazon. Chakrabarty’s study found that books written with “substantial” AI assistance made up 20 percent of Amazon’s ebook catalog, 12 percent of sales, and 10 percent of best sellers in their genre.

blocks.html_en: Yet Daggermouth stands out for more than just its popularity. The second-best-selling ebook in the data set is Inked Athena, by Nicole Fox, an author who has 418 titles listed on Amazon. Daggermouth, in contrast, appears to be one of just two novels to Wolfe’s name in 2025, and its sequel is not due out until 2027—an indication that Wolfe’s process likely involves significant amounts of genuine human craft. Iyyer said that using AI in a way that results in a novel that’s actually enjoyable to read takes “a huge amount of effort by a human author.”

blocks.html_en: Another difference: Jennifer Prokop, who reviews books for Kirkus and co-hosts Fated Mates, a popular podcast about romance novels, told me that people in her world keep talking about Daggermouth. “Nicole Fox, I’ve never heard a single soul talk about her,” she said. (Fox did not respond to a request for comment.) Prokop sees mechanical prose cropping up mostly in self-published ebooks, for which the dominant platform is Amazon’s Kindle Unlimited subscription service. Just because an ebook is charting on Kindle doesn’t mean people are devouring it. Grifters can now use AI to crank out titles by the dozen and then use all kinds of tricks to entice readers, such as buying hundreds of bogus five-star reviews and paying click farms to juice their metrics. “If you can get 10,000 people to read 10 pages of your book, and you have 300 books you’re putting out,” she said, you can make real money. “But you’re not actually writing romances people want to read.” (Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.)

blocks.html_en: If Daggermouth is AI, then maybe it’s just an outlier—a book that caught the perfect wave of social-media hype. (A series of controversies surrounding the book, including accusations of the author’s AI use and a backlash to the cover art for a special hardcover version, seemed to galvanize its fans and bring it even more attention.) The notion that AI writing requires a perfect confluence of events to top the charts is a comforting thought. But it might not be true. “Everyone thinks they can tell AI writing,” Christine Larson, a journalism professor at the University of Colorado at Boulder who studies the effect of technology on creative work, told me. “But I don’t think we can tell so much.” Privately, several authors and editors have told her that they’re using the technology to accelerate or improve their output. “I totally buy into the idea that a human working with AI can write something that is compelling,” she said. “I have absolutely no doubt that we will see more of this in the future.”

blocks.html_en: If she’s right, then the question is not about whether we’ll see AI best sellers. It’s about whether anyone involved with them will admit it. Coral Hart, a South African author who uses AI to help her publish hundreds of books a year under different pen names, told me that she works hard to keep her pseudonyms secret after she received death threats and thousands of one-star reviews following a New York Times story about her. Hart claimed that she has had successful authors join the classes that she teaches on AI writing, though she declined to name them. “Until they stop the bullying, the witch hunts, and the ousting, I don’t think authors are going to be transparent, and I don’t blame them,” Hart said. “I’m certainly not going to.”

blocks.html_en: The taboo against the use of AI in literature is understandable: Among other things, it’s wrong to take credit for a book that you didn’t write yourself. Shunning authors suspected of employing AI might work if there were any way to tell for sure—which there isn’t. That shaming ritual puts the moral burden on individual authors instead of on the mammoth corporations responsible for the system in which they’re trying to eke out a livelihood. It also tends to collapse any distinction between pure AI slop and human writing that is assisted by AI. The upshot is a state of affairs that feels untenable: AI writing can be lucrative, but only if it’s kept secret. Eventually, something’s got to give.

content_html_zh:
大多数自行出版的作家只能梦想写出像《匕首口》一样受欢迎的作品。 这部小说以蒙面精英统治的监视国家为背景，追溯了总统的儿子和受雇刺杀他的刺客之间不太可能的浪漫故事。 自从H. M。 沃尔夫将 Daggermouth 作为 Kindle 电子书上传到亚马逊，引起了病毒式的轰动。 “是我消灭了匕首，还是匕首消灭了我？” 一位 TikTok 图书影响者滔滔不绝地说。 今年二月，西蒙与舒斯特公司支付了七位数的费用，获得了该书及其续集的出版权，该书将于明年出版。

《匕首嘴》连续数月荣登《今日美国》畅销书排行榜，并在亚马逊“科幻爱情小说”类型中排名第一。 它也在一份由研究人工智能写作的学者编制的不太知名的名单中名列前茅。 在他们认为包含“大量人工智能文本”的数千本亚马逊自行出版的电子书中，没有一本比《Daggermouth》更受欢迎。

直到最近，人工智能小说还很容易被认为是废话。 从 2022 年到 2025 年，亚马逊的新书发行量几乎增加了两倍。 （这可能不是因为人类突然集体致力于文字。） 其中许多都是对现有书籍的公然模仿，似乎是为了诱骗读者购买它们。 他们的销售数字普遍微薄；评论，愤慨。 其中一些可疑的主角具有相同的名字。 去年，一本奇幻小说的读者注意到有一句台词似乎是在回应要求聊天机器人以另一位作家的风格写作的提示。 但如果像《Daggermouth》这样受人喜爱的书是用聊天机器人写的，就会引发一个尴尬的问题：人工智能小说是否会变得…… 好的？

在一项新研究中，研究人员随机选择了 14,000 多本 Kindle 电子书，并通过 AI 检测工具 Pangram 运行它们。 五分之一的人返回时，超过 25% 的内容是由 AI 编写的；根据作者与我分享的基础数据集，Daggermouth 的回报率为 60%。 他们承认，这些数字只能告诉我们这么多。 研究人员将 Pangram 标记为“人工智能生成”或“适度人工智能辅助”的文本分组在一起（后者可能意味着人工智能被用来编辑或润色人类写作，反之亦然）。 尽管 Pangram 的误报率较低，但它并不完美。

阅读：美国有一个全构图问题

因此，由石溪大学计算机科学教授 Tuhin Chakrabarty 领导的这项研究的作者设计了另一项检查。 他们扫描了每本书的文本，寻找“罕见的表达方式”——按特定顺序至少由五个单词组成的字符串——这些表达方式也出现在其他可疑的人工智能书籍中，但几乎从未出现在人类编写的书籍中。 匕首嘴有很多。 例如，第 27 章中多页性爱场景的结尾附近出现了以下句子：“他们倒在了一起，汗水湿滑的四肢纠缠在一起，心跳加速。” 同一句话逐字逐句地出现在另一位作者自行出版的另一本电子书中。 或者想想《匕首嘴》第 38 章中的这句台词：“她的脉搏在她耳边轰鸣，淹没了人群的低语声。” 另一位作者在过去三年在亚马逊上出版了 400 多本不同的书籍，其中也包含了这一内容。

该研究尚未经过同行评审，而且需要明确的是，没有明确的证据表明沃尔夫使用了人工智能。 “关于我使用生成式人工智能来编写 Daggermouth 的说法完全不真实，”沃尔夫在她的律师发出的一份声明中说。 “这本书是我自己写的。 我一直直言不讳地反对生成式人工智能以及它对作家、艺术家和创意社区的影响。 我不认为这属于写作过程。” 沃尔夫在谈到 Pangram 的局限性时补充道，“此类指控对作者来说具有真正的后果，并且不应基于已知不可靠的技术做出这些指控。” Daggermouth 出版商 Simon & Schuster 的发言人苏珊娜·劳伦斯 (Susannah Lawrence) 在一封电子邮件中告诉我，该公司支持这本书，并指出它经历了“与我们其他出版的书籍相同的编辑和制作过程”。 沃尔夫和劳伦斯都没有回答我关于《匕首口》与其他最近的电子书共有的“罕见表达方式”的问题。

研究人工智能写作的查克拉巴蒂告诉我，Daggermouth 有“太多人工智能迹象”，他无法相信这种解释。 他以第 18 章“谢谢”为例：他的研究团队将其分成 12 个部分，供 Pangram 进行评估，该工具将所有部分都分类为人工智能生成的。 （在我自己的抽查中，该工具将前几段归类为人工编写，而本章的其余部分则归类为 100% 人工智能。） 我是由马里兰大学计算机科学教授莫希特·艾耶 (Mohit Iyyer) 主持的，他没有参与这项研究。 艾耶尔是人工智能语言检测专家，他告诉我，即使考虑到 Pangram 的错误性，一本完全由人类编写的书“几乎不可能”被认定为 60% 的人工智能。 他补充说，该研究将人工智能写作与电子书销售联系起来的更广泛的方法是合理的。

无论你是否认为沃尔夫值得相信，关于《匕首口》是如何编写的同样的问题也适用于亚马逊上越来越多的其他热门作品。 Chakrabarty 的研究发现，由“大量”人工智能辅助编写的书籍占亚马逊电子书目录的 20%、销量的 12% 以及同类畅销书的 10%。

然而，Daggermouth 的脱颖而出不仅仅是因为它的受欢迎程度。 数据集中第二畅销的电子书是 Nicole Fox 的 Inked Athena，她在亚马逊上列出了 418 本书。 相比之下，《匕首口》似乎是 2025 年沃尔夫名下仅有的两部小说之一，其续集要到 2027 年才会出版——这表明沃尔夫的创作过程可能涉及大量真正的人类工艺。 艾耶尔表示，使用人工智能来创作一本真正读起来令人愉快的小说需要“人类作者付出巨大的努力”。

阅读：写作的未来很像嘻哈

另一个区别是：詹妮弗·普罗科普 (Jennifer Prokop) 为柯克斯 (Kirkus) 书评，并与人共同主持了热门浪漫小说播客《命运之友》(Fated Mates)，她告诉我，在她的世界里，人们一直在谈论匕首口。 “妮可·福克斯，我从未听过任何人谈论过她，”她说。 （福克斯没有回应置评请求。） 普罗科普认为机械散文主要出现在自行出版的电子书中，其中占主导地位的平台是亚马逊的 Kindle Unlimited 订阅服务。 一本电子书在 Kindle 上上榜并不意味着人们会如饥似渴地阅读它。 骗子现在可以使用人工智能制作出几十个标题，然后使用各种技巧来吸引读者，例如购买数百条虚假的五星级评论，并付费点击农场来提高他们的指标。 “如果你能让 10,000 人阅读你的书的 10 页，并且你已经出版了 300 本书，”她说，你就可以赚到真正的钱。 “但你实际上并不是在写人们想读的浪漫小说。” （亚马逊没有回应置评请求。）

如果《匕首口》是人工智能，那么它可能只是一个例外——一本抓住了社交媒体炒作浪潮的书。 （围绕这本书的一系列争议，包括对作者使用人工智能的指控以及对特殊精装版封面艺术的强烈反对，似乎激发了它的粉丝并给它带来了更多关注。） 人工智能写作需要事件的完美融合才能名列前茅，这一想法令人欣慰。 但这可能不是真的。 “每个人都认为他们可以告诉人工智能写作，”科罗拉多大学博尔德分校的新闻学教授克里斯汀·拉尔森（Christine Larson）告诉我，他研究技术对创造性工作的影响。 “但我认为我们不能透露这么多。” 私下里，一些作者和编辑告诉她，他们正在使用这项技术来加速或提高他们的产出。 “我完全相信使用人工智能的人可以写出一些引人注目的东西，”她说。 “我绝对毫不怀疑，我们将来会看到更多这样的事情。”

如果她是对的，那么问题不在于我们是否会看到人工智能畅销书。 问题在于与他们有关的人是否会承认这一点。 Coral Hart 是一位南非作家，她利用人工智能帮助她每年以不同的笔名出版数百本书籍。她告诉我，在《纽约时报》一篇关于她的报道后，她收到了死亡威胁和数千条一星评论，之后她就努力保密自己的笔名。 哈特声称，她已经有一些成功的作家加入了她教授的人工智能写作课程，但她拒绝透露他们的名字。 “在他们停止欺凌、政治迫害和驱逐之前，我认为作者不会保持透明，我不会责怪他们，”哈特说。 “我当然不会去。”

反对在文学中使用人工智能的禁忌是可以理解的：除此之外，将一本不是你自己写的书归功于自己是错误的。 如果有任何方法可以确定的话，回避那些怀疑使用人工智能的作者可能会起作用——但目前还没有。 这种羞辱仪式给个人作者带来了道德负担，而不是对他们试图维持生计的体系负责的庞大公司。 它还倾向于消除纯粹的人工智能书写与人工智能辅助的人类写作之间的任何区别。 结果是一种让人感觉站不住脚的状况：人工智能写作可以有利可图，但前提是保密。 最终，必须付出一些东西。
